new_d.text: Deleuze and Guattari's name, in Anti-Oedipus (1972), for desire as a process of production: an unconscious made of machines that couple flows and cut them, at work directly in natural and social production.

new_text.text: Anti-Oedipus opens with machines everywhere: “The breast is a machine that produces milk”, and the mouth is a machine coupled to it (p. 1).

The Stanford Encyclopedia article by Daniel Smith, John Protevi and Daniela Voss calls desiring-production the book's key term, a “universal primary process” beneath the natural, social and psychological realms, and stresses that no subject stands behind it and that this desire is purely positive, with no lack to make up.
Pages of Anti-Oedipus are from the translation by Robert Hurley, Mark Seem and Helen R. Lane (1977).
Desiring-machines are binary machines, one machine always coupled to another, and they link in series under the formula “and then” (p. 5).
They “work only when they break down, and by continually breaking down” (p. 8), while technical machines work only if they are not out of order (p. 31).

The fourth section, “A Materialist Psychiatry”, sets this against the logic of desire as lack, which, the authors argue, the Platonic logic of desire sets up by making us choose between production and acquisition (p. 25).

Desire, they write, “is the set of passive syntheses that engineer partial objects, flows, and bodies” (p. 26); what is missing in desire is a fixed subject (p. 26), needs derive from desire (p. 27), and lack is created and organized through social production (p. 28).
Social production, on this account, is desiring-production under determinate conditions, and libido needs no mediation to invest the productive forces (p. 29).

Hence what the authors call the fundamental problem of political philosophy, which Spinoza saw and Wilhelm Reich rediscovered, is why people fight for their servitude as though it were their salvation (p. 29).
Desiring-production works through three syntheses, connective, disjunctive and conjunctive, which the authors tie to three energies, libido, numen and voluptas (p. 41).
The Stanford article likens desiring-production to Spinoza's natura naturans and Nietzsche's will to power.

The book begins with a schizophrenic's walk, Lenz's stroll as Büchner reconstructed it, and with nature lived as a process of production (pp. 2–3), in which man and nature “are not like two opposite terms confronting each other” (pp. 4–5).

Stopping the process, or prolonging it indefinitely, produces what the authors call the artificial schizophrenic of the asylum (p. 5), and they distinguish the schizophrenic as a clinical entity from schizophrenia as a process (p. 379).
Book-length guides include Eugene Holland's Deleuze and Guattari's Anti-Oedipus: Introduction to Schizoanalysis (1999) and Ian Buchanan's Deleuze and Guattari's Anti-Oedipus: A Reader's Guide (2008).

new_d.text: A phrase Deleuze and Guattari take from Antonin Artaud: in Anti-Oedipus the unproductive surface on which desiring-production is recorded; in A Thousand Plateaus a field of intensities beneath the organism's organization.

new_text.text: The phrase comes from Antonin Artaud's To Have Done with the Judgment of God, a radio work made for French radio in late 1947 whose broadcast was cancelled before it aired.
In The Logic of Sense (1969), the Stanford Encyclopedia article notes, Deleuze drew on Artaud to name a life of intensities in motion the body without organs.
Anti-Oedipus gives it the second section of its first chapter (pp. 9–16).
Pages of Anti-Oedipus are from the translation by Robert Hurley, Mark Seem and Helen R. Lane (1977).

It forms as the third term of the connective synthesis, where production stops for a moment and “an enormous undifferentiated object” appears (p. 7): “the unproductive, the sterile, the unengendered, the unconsumable” (p. 8).
The death instinct, the authors write, is its name (p. 8), and they later call the body without organs the model of death, a model given by catatonic schizophrenia (p. 329).
It belongs to antiproduction and is perpetually reinserted into the process of production (p. 8), and it experiences the desiring-machines as “an over-all persecution apparatus” (p. 9).

By repulsion it pushes the machines away, which the authors call the paranoiac machine (p. 9); by attraction it draws them to itself, so that production seems to come from it, which they call the miraculating machine (p. 11).

It becomes the surface on which production is recorded, the site of the disjunctive synthesis (pp. 11–12), and a celibate machine joins attraction and repulsion, producing a subject as a residue beside the machines (pp. 17–18).
Society has a full body too, the socius, on which production is recorded and from which it seems to come: the earth, the tyrant, capital (p. 10).
“Capital is indeed the body without organs of the capitalist”, the authors write, “or rather of the capitalist being” (p. 10).
The intensities that fill it are all positive in relation to the zero intensity of the full body, and the authors call it an egg, crossed by thresholds and gradients (p. 19).
A Thousand Plateaus titles its sixth plateau “November 28, 1947: How Do You Make Yourself a Body without Organs?”.

There the body without organs is the enemy of the organism, a stratum that organizes the organs, and the Stanford article glosses it as “the reservoir of potentials for different patterns of bodily affect”.
The authors treat it as a practice and an experiment, and warn that wild destratification leaves emptied bodies or totalitarian and fascist ones.

new_d.text: The three processes that make up desiring-production in Anti-Oedipus, connective, disjunctive and conjunctive, each with an immanent, legitimate use and a transcendent, illegitimate use that produces Oedipus.

new_text.text: Deleuze and Guattari borrow the terms of Kant's critique: as Kant sought criteria immanent to understanding to tell legitimate from illegitimate uses of the syntheses, they denounce the illegitimate uses in psychoanalysis, whose metaphysics, they write, is Oedipus (p. 75).

The Stanford Encyclopedia article describes psychoanalysis as the transcendent use, which posits a subject behind the syntheses, and schizoanalysis as the study of their immanent use; subjects are among the products of the syntheses.
Pages of Anti-Oedipus are from the translation by Robert Hurley, Mark Seem and Helen R. Lane (1977).
The connective synthesis is the production of production, with the formula “and then” (p. 5), and its energy is libido (p. 41).

Used legitimately it is partial and nonspecific; used illegitimately it is global and specific, referring partial objects to complete objects and to persons, which the authors call the first paralogism, extrapolation (pp. 70–74).
The disjunctive synthesis is the production of recording on the body without organs, with the formula “either … or … or” (p. 12), and its energy is numen (pp. 13, 41).

Used inclusively it affirms its terms across their distance; used exclusively and restrictively it forces a choice between fixed terms, and the authors take Gregory Bateson's term double bind for this second paralogism: where Bateson saw a schizophrenizing situation, they find one that is oedipalizing par excellence (pp. 76–80; Bateson, p. 79).

The conjunctive synthesis is the production of consumption, with the formula “so it's …” (p. 17), and its energy is voluptas (pp. 16–17, 41); in it a subject is born as a residue beside the machines (p. 17).

Its legitimate use is nomadic and polyvocal and its illegitimate use segregative and biunivocal, setting up one-to-one relations between the figures of the social field and the parents, which the authors call the third paralogism, application (pp. 100–111).

Two further paralogisms follow: displacement, which concludes from the prohibition what is prohibited, while repression offers desire a falsified image of what it represses (pp. 114–115), and the afterward, which treats the actual factors of an illness as coming after family conflicts (pp. 127–129).

The book calls its syntheses passive: desire is “the set of passive syntheses” (p. 26), the term Deleuze had used in Difference and Repetition (1968) for the syntheses of time that found the present and the past (Patton's translation, pp. 71, 79).

claims.by: DR p. 71 ('this synthesis must be given a name: passive synthesis'), p. 79 (memory as 'this more profound passive synthesis')

new_text.text: Ian Buchanan argues that Anti-Oedipus's concept of passive synthesis rests on those three syntheses of time (Buchanan, pp. 50–51), and that the book's theoretical backbone was built by Deleuze in his earlier work, against the “two Deleuzes thesis” he ascribes to Alain Badiou and Slavoj Žižek (pp. 135–136).

The continuity is Buchanan's reading: Deleuze and Guattari's text never names Difference and Repetition or its syntheses of time, and only two translators' notes in the English edition point to it (pp. 393, 395).

new_d.text: The critical practice proposed in Anti-Oedipus: a materialist analysis that traces how desire invests the social field directly, set against the Oedipal reductions of psychoanalysis.

new_text.text: Anti-Oedipus calls its practice schizoanalysis, “at once a transcendental and a materialist analysis” (p. 109), and the Stanford Encyclopedia article describes it as a “materialist psychoanalysis” that studies the immanent use of the syntheses of desire.
Its target is what the article calls the “familial or ‘Oedipal’ patterning of desire” in psychoanalysis, which posits an original investment in family figures.
The unconscious, the authors write, poses only problems of use (p. 109).
Pages of Anti-Oedipus are from the translation by Robert Hurley, Mark Seem and Helen R. Lane (1977).

Schizophrenia as a process is desiring-production at the limit of social production (p. 35), and the authors distinguish it from the schizophrenic as a clinical entity produced when the process is interrupted (pp. 5, 136, 379).
The critique of psychoanalysis runs through the second chapter, “Psychoanalysis and Familialism: The Holy Family”.
The great discovery of psychoanalysis, the authors write, was the production of desire, after which a classical theater was substituted for the unconscious as a factory (p. 24).

Social repression delegates psychic repression to the family (p. 119), and Wilhelm Reich, whom the authors call the true founder of a materialist psychiatry, is credited with showing how psychic repression depends on social repression (p. 118); but, not having sufficiently formulated the concept of desiring-production, he took the desire in revolutionary investment to coincide with economic rationality, and reactionary mass investments to derive from ideology (pp. 118–119).

The fourth chapter, “Introduction to Schizoanalysis”, sets out a destructive task and two positive ones (pp. 311, 322, 340), and four theses: every investment is social (p. 342), unconscious investments of desire must be told apart from preconscious investments of interest (p. 343), the libidinal investment of the social field comes before familial investments (p. 356), and social investment has two poles, a paranoiac, fascisizing one and a schizoid, revolutionary one (p. 366).
Schizoanalysis as such, the authors add, has no political program to propose (p. 380).

Michel Foucault's preface to the English translation calls the book “an Introduction to the Non-Fascist Life” and names three adversaries: the political ascetics, among them the bureaucrats of the revolution, the technicians of desire, and fascism, including the fascism in all of us (pp. xii–xiii).
He also warns against reading it as “the new theoretical reference” (p. xii).
Guattari's working notes for the book were later published as The Anti-Oedipus Papers.

quotes.q: at once a transcendental and a materialist analysis
an Introduction to the Non-Fascist Life

new_d.text: In Anti-Oedipus, the ways social machines register flows of desire: territorial societies code them, despotic states overcode those codes, and capitalism decodes them and binds them with an axiomatic.

new_text.text: The third chapter of Anti-Oedipus, “Savages, Barbarians, Civilized Men”, is a history of social machines, and it begins with their task: to code desire is the business of the socius (p. 139).

The book's sections name three: the primitive territorial machine, the barbarian despotic machine and the civilized capitalist machine (pp. 145, 192, 222), and the Stanford Encyclopedia article describes the full body, the socius, of each, on which production is recorded and which seems to be its cause: the earth, the body of the despot, capital.
Pages of Anti-Oedipus are from the translation by Robert Hurley, Mark Seem and Helen R. Lane (1977).

The territorial machine is a socius of inscription, whose essential activity, the authors argue, is marking bodies, with exchange a secondary activity (pp. 142, 144): tattooing, excising, incising, scarifying (p. 144), in a system of cruelty and a theater of cruelty (pp. 144–145, 189).
Its graphism is independent of the voice (p. 188).

Overcoding, in the authors' words, is the operation that constitutes the essence of the State (p. 199): the despot subordinates graphism to the voice, writing appears (pp. 202–205), and the signifier emerges as the deterritorialized sign, through a biunivocalization of the old codes (pp. 205–206).

Capitalism is the only social machine built on decoded flows, putting an axiomatic of abstract quantities in the form of money in the place of codes (p. 139); it is born of the encounter of decoded flows of money-capital and of “free” labor (p. 33).
The social axiomatic is applied to private persons in the restricted family, and Oedipus becomes the private territoriality that answers capitalism's reterritorializations (pp. 263–266).

At the end of the section on the civilized capitalist machine the authors ask whether the revolutionary path is to withdraw from the world market or to go further in the movement of decoding and deterritorialization (p. 239), and answer: go further, “to ‘accelerate the process,’ as Nietzsche put it” (p. 240).

A Thousand Plateaus continues this history: the Stanford article describes the state as an “apparatus of capture” “living vampirically off of labor”, a sign of the authors' basically Marxist perspective, and the war machine as the form that “reterritorializes on deterritorialization itself”.

quotes.q: to ‘accelerate the process,’ as Nietzsche put it
